title: The Invention of the Television
summary: How Philo Farnsworth's persistent experimentation with electricity, special material, and a glass tube led to the first practical way to send moving pictures through the air.
poll: The invention of the television changed how people get news and entertainment more than almost any other invention in history.

versions.title: The Invention of the Television
versions.text:
Long ago, no one could send moving pictures through the air. People only read news in print. News took a long time to spread.

A man named Philo had a plan. He worked in his lab. He wanted to send pictures far away. He tried new ways.

Philo was not alone. Other men tried too. This way was hard. It took a long time.

Philo tried a new way. He used a small tube. The tube sent out light. This way was better.

One day, the new way worked. A moving picture showed up on a screen. This was a big change.

Today, many homes have TVs. Many watch shows fast. We thank Philo for this idea.

versions.title: The Invention of the Television
versions.text:
Long before mechanized televisions existed, no human being could truly and reliably transmit moving pictures through the air to far away places, and this seemed almost entirely impossible for a remarkably long stretch of human history indeed. People could only read news in print, which took an extraordinarily long time to disseminate around to everyone properly, accurately, and convincingly.

A man named Philo Farnsworth had a bold and genuinely ambitious plan entirely of his own, so he worked diligently in his small lab in a busy, bustling city and dreamed, quite persistently and stubbornly, of someday sending moving pictures far away using electricity. He spent many long, difficult years meticulously testing countless experimental ways to accomplish this difficult, elusive goal that had eluded so many previous experimenters before him for generations upon generations.

Philo was certainly not the sole inventor attempting this ambitious, seemingly impossible feat at that particular moment in history, since other skilled experimenters across several different countries also labored tirelessly and persistently to transmit pictures this way, frequently toiling for years without ever achieving much lasting, dependable success. This slow, maddeningly uncertain method remained quite difficult and frustrating, and it took a remarkably long time to produce even a single clear, properly moving picture that would not fade away into nothingness almost immediately.

Philo and a growing circle of fellow experimenters finally and decisively resolved to attempt something entirely novel, unconventional, and quite different altogether from anything previously attempted. He used a small glass tube coated meticulously with special material, all sealed inside a box. The tube sent out beams of light very quickly across a glowing screen. This new, meticulously engineered method turned out to be remarkably and surprisingly more effective than almost anyone had honestly anticipated at that particular moment in history.

One famous and truly historic day, Philo's new method finally worked out extremely well indeed. A clear, moving picture finally and truly appeared right there on the glowing screen at long last. This remarkable breakthrough quickly became a massive and truly lasting transformation for the entire modern world, affecting nearly every corner of daily life everywhere, from news to entertainment.

Today, countless people all around the entire world own televisions of some kind, often carried right inside their everyday pocket phones too, accessible anywhere at any moment. Many people watch shows instantly, every single day, without even pausing for a brief second thought about how it actually works. We can thank Philo for coming up with this remarkably clever and genuinely lasting idea that transformed the entire course of human history forever.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this article?
options: Print news was considered superior to television
No inventor besides Philo ever attempted to send a picture using electricity
Television had no real impact on daily life after it was invented
Philo's ambitious work led to a breakthrough in sending moving pictures
questions.why: The article centers on how Philo Farnsworth's ambitious, persistent experimentation produced a breakthrough in sending moving pictures using electricity.

wrong.A: The article presents print news as slower, not superior.
wrong.B: The article describes other inventors who also attempted this.
wrong.C: The article shows television transforming daily life afterward.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why did earlier attempts to send pictures largely fail?
options: They were considered too colorful for serious inventors to use
They were banned by governments across every country
They lacked a reliable way for electricity to form a lasting picture
They required no material or experimentation whatsoever
questions.why: The article explains that earlier attempts lacked a reliable method for electricity to form a lasting, moving picture, making them frustrating and unsuccessful.

wrong.A: Color is never discussed as a reason for failure.
wrong.B: No government ban on these attempts is mentioned.
wrong.D: Material and experimentation were part of these attempts, just unsuccessfully.

questions.stem: What specific combination enabled Philo's method to finally succeed?
options: Painted canvas alone, with no material
A glass tube, material, and controlled electricity
Borrowed printing tools with no electricity involved
A sealed box filled with water
questions.why: The article describes Philo's method as combining a glass tube, special material, and carefully controlled electricity to finally succeed.

wrong.A: Material was essential to the method, as described.
wrong.C: Electricity was central to the method's success.
wrong.D: Water is never mentioned as part of the method.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about innovation from the fact that multiple inventors in different countries pursued this same frustrating goal?
options: A shared, difficult problem can inspire independent efforts toward similar solutions
Only inventors in one particular country are capable of true innovation in the world
Most important inventions in history have had one true creator
Independent experimentation rarely leads to useful breakthroughs
questions.why: Multiple inventors in different countries pursuing this goal suggests that a widely shared, difficult problem can inspire separate efforts toward similar solutions.

wrong.B: Inventors in several countries pursued this goal, not just one.
wrong.C: The article shows multiple people contributing to this shared goal.
wrong.D: Philo's own experimentation clearly led to a real breakthrough.

questions.stem: Why does the article emphasize the many frustrating years Philo spent testing before succeeding?
options: To show that experimentation results in total failure
To argue that testing an idea repeatedly is generally pointless
To prove that Philo worked without any plan
To suggest that persistence through difficulty leads to breakthroughs
questions.why: Emphasizing the many frustrating years of testing suggests that persistence through difficulty was essential to Philo's eventual breakthrough.

wrong.A: The article shows testing eventually leading to success.
wrong.B: The article presents this testing as essential, not pointless.
wrong.C: Philo's careful, repeated testing shows a clear, deliberate plan.

questions.stem: In the article, what does "ambitious" most precisely describe about Philo's plan?
options: That it aimed at something difficult and far-reaching
That it was extremely easy to accomplish quickly
That it required no material or experimentation
That it was abandoned almost immediately after starting
questions.why: The article uses "ambitious" to show that Philo's plan aimed at something difficult and far-reaching, not something simple.

wrong.B: Ambitious describes a difficult goal, not an easy one.
wrong.C: Material and experimentation were central to his plan.
wrong.D: Philo persisted for years rather than abandoning his plan.

questions.stem: How does the article's structure support its central idea about this remarkable achievement?
options: It randomly jumps between unrelated inventions with no clear order
It focuses on describing Philo's personal childhood memories
It presents the early failures, experimentation, and breakthrough in order
It only compares the prices of modern televisions across different brands
questions.why: The article's sequence, from frustrating early failures through experimentation to lasting breakthrough, reinforces its central idea about a historic achievement.

wrong.A: The structure follows one invention in a clear, logical order.
wrong.B: Philo's childhood beyond his work is not the article's focus.
wrong.D: Modern television prices are never discussed in the article.

questions.stem: What effect did Philo's breakthrough have on how people get moving pictures today?
options: It made sending pictures scarcer and far more difficult than before
It allowed people to watch moving pictures almost instantly and easily
It limited picture-sending to only trained inventors
It had no measurable effect on how people get moving pictures
questions.why: Because Philo's breakthrough proved moving pictures could be sent reliably, it eventually led to the instant, easy television people rely on today.

wrong.A: The article shows picture-sending becoming far easier, not scarcer.
wrong.C: The article shows television spreading widely, not staying limited to inventors.
wrong.D: The article clearly links this breakthrough to today's television.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how earlier failed attempts, repeated experimentation, and persistence shaped Philo Farnsworth's breakthrough, and explain its lasting impact. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: Did you mention earlier, frustrating attempts to send pictures?
Did you explain the role of material and repeated experimentation?
Did you connect the breakthrough to its lasting impact on television today?
HIGH.modelAnswer: Philo Farnsworth's breakthrough grew out of years of frustrating, largely unsuccessful attempts by inventors across several countries who shared his ambitious goal of sending moving pictures through the air. Working patiently in his own lab, Philo tested countless combinations of material, glass tubes, and carefully controlled electricity, enduring repeated failures along the way. His eventual success finally produced a clear, moving picture on a screen, proving that sending pictures with electricity was truly possible. That remarkable breakthrough transformed how people experience news and entertainment, leading directly to the instant, effortless television that billions of people now rely on every single day without a second thought.

LOW.stem: What problem was Philo trying to solve?
options: How to send moving pictures through the air instead of printing news
How to make his lab bigger
How to sell more glass tubes
How to print newspapers more slowly
LOW.why: Philo's whole goal was to send moving pictures through the air, instead of relying only on printed news.

wrong.B: Lab size is not Philo's goal in the article.
wrong.C: Selling tubes is not mentioned as his goal.
wrong.D: The article shows Philo wanting a faster way, not a slower one.

LOW.stem: Why did it matter that a moving picture could finally show up on a screen?
options: It proved that sending pictures through the air was possible
It proved that printed news was no longer allowed
It proved that screens could never be used again
It proved that electricity was dangerous to use
LOW.why: The appearance of a moving picture proved that sending pictures through the air using electricity was truly possible.

wrong.B: Printed news is not banned in the article.
wrong.C: Screens were used, not avoided, after this success.
wrong.D: Danger from electricity is never mentioned in the article.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about Philo from how many times he tried a new way?
options: He gave up quickly when his first idea did not work
He kept trying patiently until he found a way that worked
He did not care whether his idea worked
He worked completely alone with no one else trying
LOW.why: The article shows Philo trying many new ways, which shows he worked patiently until his idea finally worked.

wrong.A: The opposite is true; he kept trying instead of giving up.
wrong.C: He clearly cared, since he kept testing for a long time.
wrong.D: The article mentions other men also trying to send pictures.

LOW.stem: Why does the article end by talking about TVs today?
options: To show how much Philo's idea changed how we watch shows
To say that TVs no longer work
To explain that people read print again instead
To prove that nobody watches shows anymore
LOW.why: Ending with today's TVs helps readers see how much Philo's idea changed the way we watch shows.

wrong.B: The article shows TVs still working well today.
wrong.C: The article shows people watching TVs, not reading print instead.
wrong.D: The article says many people watch shows, meaning people still do.

MID.stem: What does it suggest that several inventors in different countries struggled with the same problem?
options: Only Philo ever cared about sending pictures
A shared, difficult problem can inspire many independent attempts
Every inventor secretly copied the exact same method
Sending a picture through the air was always simple
MID.why: The fact that many inventors in different countries faced the same challenge shows how a shared, difficult problem can inspire many independent attempts.

wrong.A: Other inventors also cared and tried.
wrong.C: The article never claims inventors copied each other.
wrong.D: The article shows this problem as quite difficult, not simple.

MID.stem: Based on the article, what likely made Philo's method succeed where simple attempts could not?
options: It combined electricity, special material, and a tube in a reliable way
It used no electricity or material at all
It required far more time than any other method
It made only temporary pictures that faded instantly
MID.why: Philo's method combined electricity, special material, and a tube in a way that reliably produced a moving picture, unlike earlier attempts.

wrong.B: Electricity and material were key parts of the method.
wrong.C: The method was remarkably faster, not slower, than earlier attempts.
wrong.D: The method produced lasting pictures, not fading ones.

MID.stem: Why might the article mention how difficult early attempts were before describing Philo's success?
options: To help readers understand why Philo's breakthrough mattered so much
To prove that television should remain difficult
To show that Philo wanted pictures to fade quickly
To explain that other inventors were paid very well
MID.why: By explaining how difficult early attempts were, the article helps readers understand why Philo's breakthrough was such an important achievement.

wrong.B: The article shows the opposite; Philo made this easier.
wrong.C: Philo's goal was lasting pictures, not fading ones.
wrong.D: Inventor pay is never discussed in the article.

MID.stem: What is the most likely reason the article ends by describing how people watch shows instantly today?
options: To show how far television has come since Philo's time
To argue that televisions should be banned
To prove that nobody watches shows anymore
To explain exactly how phone screens are built
MID.why: By pointing out how quickly we can watch shows today, the article highlights the huge progress made since Philo's original breakthrough.

wrong.B: The article presents television as a valuable, lasting achievement.
wrong.C: The article says people watch shows every day, meaning they still do.
wrong.D: Modern phone screen construction is not explained in the article.

HIGH.stem: What does the article imply about the relationship between frustrating failure and historic breakthroughs?
options: Failure has no meaningful connection to eventual breakthroughs
Repeated, frustrating failure can be a necessary part of reaching a historic breakthrough
A breakthrough always happens on the very first attempt
Other inventors should have stopped testing after one failed attempt
HIGH.why: Philo's many frustrating failed experiments before success suggest that repeated failure is often necessary on the path to a breakthrough.

wrong.A: The article closely links his many failures to the eventual breakthrough.
wrong.C: The article describes many failed attempts before success, not an immediate one.
wrong.D: Other inventors continued testing despite earlier setbacks, as the article shows.

HIGH.stem: Why might historians discuss Philo alongside other inventors who also tried to send pictures rather than crediting only him?
options: Because independent experimentation by multiple inventors shaped the eventual breakthrough
Because only Philo ever built a working television of any kind
Because Philo and other inventors worked in the exact same lab
Because sending a picture was achieved purely by accident with no testing
HIGH.why: Crediting multiple inventors reflects how independent experimentation by several people shaped the path toward the eventual breakthrough.

wrong.B: Other inventors also tried to send pictures, just without success.
wrong.C: Philo worked in his own separate lab.
wrong.D: The article describes deliberate, careful experimentation, not accident.

HIGH.stem: What underlying assumption does the article make about why sending moving pictures mattered so much?
options: That people valued being able to see events and shows from far away
That people had no real interest in seeing far-away events
That people preferred pictures to remain rare and hard to send
That people were indifferent to how pictures were produced
HIGH.why: The article's emphasis on sending moving pictures far away implies that people valued the chance to see events and shows from a distance.

wrong.B: The article shows strong demand once moving pictures became easy to send.
wrong.C: The article presents widely available pictures as a positive outcome, not a loss.
wrong.D: The article links the method directly to how pictures could be shared.

HIGH.stem: How does the article's closing focus on how instantly we watch shows today serve its larger purpose?
options: It suggests a frustrating, historic breakthrough can become an unnoticed part of everyday life
It argues that television ultimately failed its original purpose
It proves that nobody values television enough to watch it today
It shows that print news remains the most common way to get pictures
HIGH.why: By noting how instantly we watch shows today, the article suggests that Philo's historic breakthrough became such an essential, unnoticed part of daily life.

wrong.B: The article presents television as a celebrated, lasting success.
wrong.C: The article shows people watching shows constantly, implying high value.
wrong.D: The article explicitly contrasts modern instant television with the slower methods of the past.
